claims.text: Elevated-temperature wear instability in FeNiCrCoCu coatings on a Cu matrix is caused by a critical thermal-activation threshold for stacking-fault dissociation.
Crossing this threshold shifts deformation from dislocation-mediated plasticity to lattice softening, atomic disorder, and amorphization.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has a stable FCC solid-solution structure at 300 K.
At 300 K, the coating has high dislocation density and well-defined stacking faults.
Stacking-fault energy and dislocation-core width mediate the temperature-dependent wear transition.
The structural evolution proceeds from separated partial dislocations and stable stacking faults to full-dislocation dissociation and amorphization.
At low temperature, sluggish diffusion and lattice distortion stabilize stacking faults and impede dislocation motion.
Stabilized stacking faults and impeded dislocation motion maintain low-temperature wear resistance.
Increasing temperature reduces the stacking-fault energy barrier.
Thermal activation promotes conversion of partial dislocations into full dislocations and accelerates atomic diffusion.
Rapid diffusion causes lattice collapse and amorphization, especially at grain boundaries and highly stressed contact zones.
Amorphization can dominate plasticity in nanocrystalline HEAs below a critical grain size.
Lattice collapse removes defect barriers to plastic flow and thereby causes a sharp decline in wear resistance.
The critical temperature is likely between 600 K and 750 K.
At the critical temperature, wear rate increases exponentially.
Below the critical temperature, wear is governed by abrasion, stable oxide layers, and dislocation slip.
Above the critical temperature, severe plastic flow, surface amorphization, and rapid lattice disorder dominate wear.
Above the critical temperature, material-loss rates become comparable to or greater than those of pure metals.
The room-temperature high modulus and stable wear rate arise from high-entropy and lattice-distortion effects.
The proposed mechanism is specific to temperature-sensitive FCC HEAs and may not apply to BCC-dominant HEAs, where twinning can dominate.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome states that wear rate increases sharply or exponentially above the threshold, whereas the falsification rule refers to a 'sharp decline' in wear rate. A decline in wear resistance would imply an increase, not a decline, in wear rate.
